title: Sukkot: guests from the past
hookLine: each night mystical guests are welcomed: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and in many homes Sarah and others

cards: The first night of Sukkot. The hut is up: three walls of canvas or plywood, a roof of branches with stars showing through, paper chains made by children, a string of lights. The family squeezes in around a folding table.
And before the meal, in many homes, someone reads an invitation. Not to the neighbors. To Abraham.
Please come in, take your seat. Tonight Abraham leads the guests.

teach.b: The custom comes from the Zohar, the great book of Jewish mysticism. It calls these visitors ushpizin, an Aramaic word for guests. Seven of them: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Joseph and David.
All seven come every night, the mystics say, but each night a different one leads. Why these seven? Many of them were wanderers.
Abraham left home for a land he didn't know. Jacob fled. Joseph was carried off to Egypt.
Moses led a people through the desert in huts. David hid in caves. They know what it's like to live in a temporary shelter.
In many homes today, women are welcomed too, ushpizot: Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Leah, Miriam, Abigail, Esther, or other lists, depending on the community. And the Zohar doesn't stop at the invitation.

teach.h: THEIR PORTION GOES TO THE POOR.
teach.b: It says the guests' portion belongs to the poor.
Set a lovely table for Abraham with no one hungry eating from it, and the guests get up and leave. Abraham, after all, was well-known for running out of his tent to welcome strangers.
So you honor the heroes of the past by feeding someone in the present. Some families leave an empty chair. Others hang the names on the sukkah wall.
Many make sure an actual guest is at the table every night.

how: On each night of Sukkot many families recite an invitation to the ushpizin in the sukkah, and many add women guests (ushpizot); hosting real guests and giving to the poor is considered part of the custom.

games.q: you've invited Abraham to your sukkah and set a beautiful table. but you've invited no one in need. what does the Zohar say happens?
o: the guests get up and leave.
games.why: the guests' portion belongs to the poor. honor the past by feeding someone in the present.

practice: Picture your table, wherever it is, and welcome one person from the past to it: a grandparent, a teacher, a figure from the stories.
Then ask who, alive and nearby, might need a seat there: someone new in town, someone alone, someone struggling. If you pray, you can ask for an open door; if not, just hold that person in mind.

wordCard.voice: Ushpizin. Guests. The seven figures from the past welcomed into the sukkah, one leading each night, whose portion goes to the poor.

carryVoice: Your line: invite the guests. The past is honored at a table set for the present. See you tomorrow.
